content: Efforts should focus on improving the implementation of guidelines for estimating the requirements of substances under international control. Collaboration with UNICEF and other relevant partners is essential to promote and implement palliative care for children. Monitoring the global status of palliative care is necessary, including evaluating progress in various initiatives and programs in partnership with Member States and international organizations. Member States should be encouraged to allocate adequate funding and enhance cooperation for palliative care programs and research, particularly in resource-limited countries, in alignment with the 2014–2015 Program Budget addressing palliative care. Research on effective palliative care models in lowand middle-income countries should be promoted, with an emphasis on identifying and applying good practices. Progress on the implementation of this resolution should be reported to the Sixty-ninth World Health Assembly in 2016. The International Narcotics Control Board and the World Health Organization have developed a guide for estimating the requirements of substances under international control, published by the United Nations in 2012. Strategic planning for palliative care involves identifying actionable steps within home institutions, as outlined in group work and discussions from the Global Program of Harvard Medical School’s Center for Palliative Care and Massachusetts General Hospital in 2017. Training programs for implementing palliative care nursing in home institutions include lectures, group work, and final examinations, as demonstrated by the University of Medicine & Pharmacy in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, and Harvard Medical School’s Global Program. A WHO guide for planners, implementers, and managers provides a basic curriculum for training community health workers (CHWs) in palliative care. This curriculum includes eight 30-minute sessions covering topics such as the definition of palliative care, CHWs’ responsibilities to patients, understanding patients’ medical, psychosocial, and spiritual needs, effective communication, recognizing uncontrolled symptoms, knowing when and how to report to supervisors, resilience and self-care, and grief and bereavement support. These sessions are adapted from the Institute of Palliative Medicine’s workbook for carers, developed in collaboration with the WHO Collaborating Centre for Community Participation in Palliative Care and Long-Term Care in Kerala, India. Bereavement support involves providing psychological, spiritual, or emotional counseling to individuals grieving the loss of a loved one. Community health workers (CHWs) are members of the communities they serve, selected by the community, accountable to it, and supported by the health system, though not necessarily part of it. They receive shorter training compared to professional health workers. Strengthening health systems involves identifying and implementing policy and practice changes to improve a country’s ability to address health challenges. This includes initiatives that enhance access, coverage, quality, and efficiency of health services. Hospice care refers to organizations or institutions dedicated to providing inpatient or outpatient palliative care for patients nearing the end of life. Internally displaced persons (IDPs) are individuals forced to flee their homes without crossing international borders. They seek safety in nearby towns, schools, settlements, camps, or even forests and fields. IDPs, displaced by internal conflict or natural disasters, represent the largest group assisted by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR). Unlike refugees, IDPs are not protected by international law and remain under the jurisdiction of their home country. Intersectoral action involves engaging multiple sectors beyond health to design and implement public policies that improve health care and quality of life. People-centered health services are designed to incorporate the perspectives of individuals, families, and communities, emphasizing their role as participants and beneficiaries of trusted health systems that respond to their needs and preferences in a humane and holistic manner. This approach requires education and support to empower individuals to make decisions and participate in their care, focusing on health needs rather than diseases. A refugee is someone forced to flee their country due to persecution, war, or violence, with a well-founded fear of persecution based on race, religion, nationality, political opinion, or social group membership. Refugees often cannot return home due to safety concerns. War, ethnic, tribal, and religious violence are leading causes of refugee displacement. Serious health-related suffering (SHS) occurs when suffering associated with illness or injury cannot be alleviated without medical intervention and compromises physical, social, or emotional functioning. Palliative care should prioritize relieving SHS associated with life-limiting or life-threatening conditions or end-of-life care. Social determinants of health refer to the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age, shaped by the distribution of money, power, and resources at various levels. These determinants are responsible for health inequities, which are unfair and avoidable differences in health status within and between countries. Health services under UHC include health promotion initiatives (e.g., anti-tobacco policies, emergency preparedness), disease prevention activities (e.g., vaccination), and the provision of treatment, rehabilitation, and palliative care (e.g., symptom relief and end-of-life care) of sufficient quality to be effective.
